about: Curated by The Owlmanac: one plain entry per addition, newest first. Add an entry whenever something visitors can see ships.

items.p: Every section now opens with its own engraving-style illustration, and the turning emblem appears on menu pages, while things load, when you finish a mission and beside the logo. The picture glossary has two new tabs (Inside the Earth, Sky & light), and every mission card shows its challenge level.

The Owlmanac Observatory is new and still changing; the Beta mark by the logo says so. Missions now say what changes with each age, lessons read aloud with the most natural voice your device has (and you can pick another), the Moon reading sits at the top right of the map instead of on the globe, and What's new keeps a way back after you try something.

items.t: A tenth mission: Inside the Earth
items.p: How earthquake waves reveal the crust, mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core, for all four ages, with this week's quakes at their real depth and the true-scale cutaway.

items.t: Richer menu pages, and small fixes
items.p: Each menu page now opens with what is happening right now, and every section card carries a live figure. Pressing a menu item or banner card again closes its side panel. Close-up imagery is now called Orthoimagery, and the map, imagery and lighting choices explain themselves when you rest the pointer on them. Contact has a Make a suggestion link.

Click a menu's name (People, Planet, Space, Sky tonight, Classroom, About) to see every section in it on one page, each with a line on what it holds. On a phone, the first item in each menu does the same.
All ten missions, class mode, worksheets with answer keys and the daily warm-up are free with no accounts, and stay free. Teachers can ask to hear if optional tools for schools ever arrive.

items.t: Classroom: a students' side and an educators' side
items.p: Nine missions on the live globe, each told four ways for ages 6 to adult, now with an educators' tab: class mode for the projector, a printable worksheet and answer key for every mission, today's warm-up question and the matching science standards.
Volcanoes and plates, the Moon and its phases, the scale of space, climate and ice, and animal migration. Every fact was checked against the source it cites, twice.

items.t: Contact, the weekly letter, and this page
items.p: Write to us, report a problem, or sign up for the weekly letter before its first issue.

items.t: The edge of the observable universe as a globe
items.p: The oldest light, mapped by ESA's Planck satellite, now wraps a lit sphere you can turn. Every tour ends on the Owlmanac emblem; drag it to spin it.
A daily game: five owls hidden on the real globe, each smaller than the last, with clues from real places and one live event.
Learn became Classroom, with the Classroom itself first. Sources, Keep it free and About moved to their own About menu. Pinch-zoom now heads for the spot under your fingers.
A short flight from Earth past the planets to where Voyager 1 is today, ending over its shoulder looking back at the Sun. Start it from the Voyager countdown.

items.t: A scale slider, and view buttons everywhere
items.p: With the panels tucked away, a slider on the right flies you from Earth to the edge. The Earth, Moon, Solar System, Milky Way and Cosmic web buttons now stay in the space views.
Open Records full page for tabs, counts and a search box; every record folds into a card.
Live lightning now adds EUMETSAT's Meteosat-12 Lightning Imager to NOAA's GOES satellites over the Americas.

items.t: Explain options, and the Moon's dark side
items.p: A switch at the top of Filter options turns on short explanations. In the Moon view, Light the dark side shows the whole surface.
History from below, in the words of the people it happened to, now from 416 BC to the 1970s.
A wordless flight from outside the observable universe in to Earth and back out, with its own score.
